---
title: "Analysis 2: What happens when we replace different residues with alanine?"
author: "Luis Sebastian Galán, Laura Grenaa Jensen, Taniya Dey and Thota Kanishka Rao"
format: html
---

## What are we looking at?

We want to see which types of amino acids show the biggest changes in
binding when replaced with alanine. We first compare the chemical groups
using all alanine mutations together. Then we check which differences
are still there after accounting for the chain and structure.

We use 328 experimental $\Delta \Delta G$ measurements. A positive value means that the
mutation weakened binding compared with the original complex.

## Select and describe the alanine mutations

We select mutations to alanine using to_alanine from the augmentation
step. We keep rows with a recorded $\Delta \Delta G$, chemical group, mutation
location, and structure pdb so we can use the same rows in every model.

```{r}
#| label: select-alanine-mutations

library("tidyverse")
library("here")

dat_aug <- read_csv(here("data", "03_dat_aug.csv"))

dat_alanine <- dat_aug |>
  filter(
    to_alanine,
    mut_from != "A",) |>
  drop_na(ddg, type_from, mutation_category, pdb) |>
  mutate(
    type_from = factor(type_from),
    mutation_category = factor(mutation_category),
    pdb = factor(pdb)
  )
```

Four of the 328 measurements are exactly 8 kcal/mol, which in this dataset means the assay could not detect binding weaker than this, so the true $\Delta \Delta G$ is ≥ 8. All four are aromatic (W, Y) or positive (R, H) residues. We keep these values as 8, which means the mean estimates for those two groups are lower bounds for the true mean.

## Which amino acids had the highest mean $\Delta \Delta G$?
We start by comparing the mean experimental $\Delta \Delta G$ for each starting
amino acid. Some amino acids were measured only once or twice, so we
show how many measurements and complexes are behind each mean.

```{r}
#| label: alanine-by-amino-acid

alanine_summary <- dat_alanine |>
  group_by(mut_from, type_from) |>
  summarise(
    n_measurements = n(),
    n_complexes = n_distinct(pdb),
    mean_ddg = mean(ddg),
    median_ddg = median(ddg),
    n_capped = sum(ddg == 8),
    sd_ddg = sd(ddg),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    se_ddg = sd_ddg / sqrt(n_measurements),
    df = if_else(n_measurements > 1, n_measurements - 1, NA_real_),
    margin = qt(0.975, df = df) * se_ddg,
    ci_lower = mean_ddg - margin,
    ci_upper = mean_ddg + margin
  ) |>
  select(-sd_ddg, -se_ddg, -df, -margin) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_ddg))

alanine_summary
```

We compare the mean experimental $\Delta \Delta G$ for each starting amino acid.
The labels show how many measurements and complexes each mean is
based on. The lines show $95\%$ confidence intervals. Amino acids with
only one measurement are shown as a point without an interval.

```{r}
#| label: fig-alanine-by-amino-acid
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

alanine_summary |>
  mutate(mut_from = fct_reorder(mut_from, mean_ddg)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_ddg, y = mut_from, colour = type_from)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = ci_lower, xend = ci_upper, yend = mut_from),
    linewidth = 0.7,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_measurements)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean experimental ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    y = "Starting amino acid",
    colour = "Chemical group",
    size = "Measurements"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


## Do the chemical groups differ?

Some amino acids had only a few measurements, so we group the mutations by the chemical properties of the starting amino acid. We start with a one-way ANOVA to test whether mean $\Delta \Delta G$ differs across the chemical groups. At this point we pool mutations from all locations
and structures.

```{r}
#| label: test-pooled-chemical-groups

model_pooled <- lm(
  ddg ~ type_from,
  data = dat_alanine
)

anova(model_pooled)
```

Mean ΔΔG differed between at least two chemical groups in the pooled
analysis (`F(5, 322) = 4.60, p = 0.000455`).


## Which differences remain after adjusting for location and structure?

Some chemical groups may have been tested more often on certain chains
or in certain structures. To account for this, we fit two models that
both include mutation location (`mutation_category`) and PDB ID
(`pdb`). We add chemical group to the second model and test whether it
improves the fit.


```{r}
#| label: test-adjusted-chemical-groups

model_without_chemistry <- lm(
  ddg ~ mutation_category + pdb,
  data = dat_alanine
)

model_adjusted <- lm(
  ddg ~ type_from + mutation_category + pdb,
  data = dat_alanine
)

anova(model_without_chemistry, model_adjusted)
```

Adding chemical group improved the model fit after accounting for
mutation location and structure (`F(5, 302) = 3.94, p = 0.00177`).

We then compare the chemical groups two at a time in both the pooled and
adjusted models. We use Holm's method to adjust the p-values within each
set of comparisons.

The estimates are mean differences in kcal/mol. For example, a positive
estimate for `aromatic - polar` means the aromatic group had a higher
estimated mean $\Delta \Delta G$

```{r}
#| label: compare-pooled-and-adjusted-pairs

pooled_means <- emmeans::emmeans(model_pooled, specs = "type_from")
adjusted_means <- emmeans::emmeans(model_adjusted, specs = "type_from")

pooled_pairs <- emmeans::contrast(
  pooled_means,
  method = "pairwise",
  adjust = "holm"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(
    contrast,
    pooled_difference = estimate,
    pooled_p_adjusted = p.value
  )

adjusted_pairs <- emmeans::contrast(
  adjusted_means,
  method = "pairwise",
  adjust = "holm"
) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(
    contrast,
    adjusted_difference = estimate,
    adjusted_se = SE,
    adjusted_p_adjusted = p.value
  )

pairwise_comparison <- pooled_pairs |>
  left_join(adjusted_pairs, by = "contrast") |>
  arrange(adjusted_p_adjusted)

pairwise_comparison
```

After accounting for mutation location and structure, two pairs had
Holm-adjusted p-values below 0.05. Mean $\Delta \Delta G$ was `0.98 kcal/mol` higher
for aromatic-to-alanine mutations and `0.79 kcal/mol` higher for
positive-to-alanine mutations, both compared with polar-to-alanine
mutations. The aromatic–polar difference decreased from `1.25` to
`0.98 kcal/mol` after adjustment, while the positive–polar difference
stayed about the same.

## Do the differences vary by mutation location?

The adjusted model gives one difference per pair of chemical groups. We
now test whether those differences vary between the heavy chain, light
chain, and antigen. For example, the gap between aromatic and polar
residues could be larger on the heavy chain than on the light chain.

We first check how many rows we have for each combination. A combination
with few or no rows gives us little information about that comparison.

```{r}
#| label: count-mutations-by-location

dat_alanine |>
  count(mutation_category, type_from) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = type_from,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )
```

The aromatic and polar groups were represented at all three locations,
with at least 17 rows per group at each location. The hydrophobic group
had no rows on the heavy chain and two on the light chain. There
were no rows from the negative group on the light chain. This limits
what we can say about those groups on the antibody chains.

```{r}
#| label: test-chemical-group-by-location

model_location_interaction <- lm(
  ddg ~ type_from * mutation_category + pdb,
  data = dat_alanine
)

anova(model_adjusted, model_location_interaction)
```

Adding the interaction improved the model fit when all rows were
included (`F(8, 294) = 2.36, p = 0.018`). This suggests that some
chemical-group differences varied across locations. This overall test
doesn’t tell us which pairs varied. We use the next plot to look at the
patterns on the heavy chain, light chain, and antigen.

The plot shows the observed $\Delta \Delta G$ values at each location. We use the same
scale in all three panels so the patterns are easy to compare.

```{r}
#| label: fig-alanine-chemistry-by-location

dat_alanine |>
  ggplot(aes(x = type_from, y = ddg, fill = type_from)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ mutation_category,
    ncol = 1,
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      ab_heavy = "Heavy chain",
      ab_light = "Light chain",
      antigen = "Antigen"
    ))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Chemical group of the original amino acid",
    y = "Experimental ΔΔG (kcal/mol)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The aromatic group had a higher observed median $\Delta \Delta G$ than the polar group
in all three panels. The gap looked larger on the heavy chain than on
the light chain. These are the observed values, so we use the plot to
describe the pattern. A separate comparison would be needed to test
whether the aromatic–polar gap itself differs between chains.

## Do the differences vary by structure?

We do the same check for structure pdb. We first count how many chemical
groups are represented in each structure. A structure with only one
group gives us no direct comparison between groups within that
structure.

```{r}
#| label: count-groups-by-structure

dat_alanine |>
  distinct(pdb, type_from) |>
  count(pdb, name = "n_chemical_groups") |>
  count(n_chemical_groups, name = "n_structure_pdbs")
```

Seven of the 19 structure pdbs had data for all six chemical groups. Two
had data for only one group, so they could not contribute a
within-structure comparison. The remaining structures let us compare
some of the groups.

```{r}
#| label: test-chemical-group-by-structure

model_structure_interaction <- lm(
  ddg ~ type_from * pdb + mutation_category,
  data = dat_alanine
)

anova(model_adjusted, model_structure_interaction)
```

We found no clear evidence that the chemical-group differences varied by
structure pdb (`F(63, 239) = 0.96, p = 0.557`). Since only seven
structures had data for all six groups, some differences were hard to
compare across structures. In the next plot, we look at the
aromatic–polar difference in the structures where both groups were
tested.

We use aromatic and polar residues as an example in the plot below. For
each structure with both groups, we subtract the observed polar median
from the observed aromatic median. A point to the right of zero means
the aromatic group had the higher median $\Delta \Delta G$ in that structure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-aromatic-polar-by-structure
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

structure_comparison <- dat_alanine |>
  filter(type_from %in% c("aromatic", "polar")) |>
  group_by(pdb, type_from) |>
  summarise(
    median_ddg = median(ddg),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = type_from,
    values_from = median_ddg
  ) |>
  drop_na(aromatic, polar) |>
  mutate(median_difference = aromatic - polar)

structure_comparison |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = median_difference,
    y = fct_reorder(pdb, median_difference)
  )) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Aromatic median − polar median ΔΔG (kcal/mol)",
    y = "Structure pdb"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Of the 15 structure IDs with both groups, 12 had a higher median $\Delta \Delta G$ for
aromatic-to-alanine mutations, two had a higher median for
polar-to-alanine mutations, and one had the same median. The difference
went in the same direction in most structures. These are observed
medians, and the plot does not adjust for mutation location.

## What did we find?

After accounting for mutation location and structure, mean $\Delta \Delta G$ was 0.98
kcal/mol higher for aromatic-to-alanine mutations and 0.79 kcal/mol
higher for positive-to-alanine mutations than for polar-to-alanine
mutations (Holm-adjusted `p = 0.00142` and `p = 0.0282`).

With all rows included, the differences varied by mutation location (`p
= 0.018`). Both pairs differed on the heavy chain, and only
positive–polar differed on the light chain. The direct comparisons
between locations were inconclusive. We found no clear evidence that the
differences varied by structure (`p = 0.557`). For the aromatic and
positive groups, the capped values can only push the true mean up, so the
reported differences relative to polar are, if anything, understated.
